questions.q: A 7-billion-parameter model stored in FP16 is only about 14GB. Why does training it still require far more than 80GB of GPU memory?
options: FP16 weights silently double in size the moment training starts
Training also has to hold gradients and optimizer state (e.g. Adam's per-parameter moment estimates, usually in FP32), plus activations — together far larger than the weights alone
GPU memory is only usable at half capacity once CUDA is loaded
It doesn't — 14GB is already enough to train that model on a single GPU
questions.explain: Parameters are the smallest line item. Gradients match parameter size, and Adam's optimizer state (two FP32 moments per parameter) typically adds roughly 4x the parameter memory on top — before activations are even counted.

questions.q: Why does Adam's optimizer state usually consume more memory than the model's parameters themselves?
options: Adam keeps a first and second moment estimate per parameter, typically in FP32, which adds roughly two full-precision copies of every parameter on top of the weights and gradients
Adam stores a complete copy of the entire training dataset in GPU memory
Adam requires activations to be duplicated across every layer
Adam's optimizer state is actually smaller than the parameters, not larger
questions.explain: Adam tracks per-parameter first and second moment estimates for stability, usually kept in FP32 even when the model itself trains in mixed precision — that's the single biggest memory line item in most training setups.

questions.q: What makes activation memory different from parameter, gradient, and optimizer-state memory?
options: Activation memory is fixed and never changes regardless of training configuration
Activation memory scales with batch size and sequence length, not just model/parameter size, and can rival or exceed the weights themselves at long context lengths
Activations are stored on CPU RAM exclusively and never touch the GPU
Activations only exist during inference, never during training
questions.explain: Unlike parameters, gradients, and optimizer state (which scale with model size), activations scale with batch size and sequence length — making them a major, variable memory cost, especially for transformers with long context.

questions.q: A model fits entirely in one GPU's memory, including optimizer state and activations. Why might it still need multiple GPUs to train?
options: Models that fit in memory never need more than one GPU under any circumstances
A single GPU cannot legally be used for training under any cloud provider's terms of service
Training compute scales with both model size and dataset size; processing trillions of tokens on one GPU can take an impractical number of GPU-days even when memory isn't the limiter
GPUs cannot run backpropagation unless networked with at least one other GPU
questions.explain: Memory and time are separate pressures. Even a model that fits comfortably can require splitting the work across many GPUs simply to finish training in a practical amount of wall-clock time.

questions.q: Based on this lesson, which parallelism strategy addresses which problem?
options: Model parallelism and data parallelism solve identical problems and are interchangeable in every scenario
Data parallelism is used when the model doesn't fit on a GPU; model parallelism is used when training simply takes too long
Both strategies apply only to inference, never to training
Data parallelism replicates the model across GPUs to speed up training when the model already fits; model parallelism splits the model itself across GPUs when it does not fit
questions.explain: Data parallelism tackles the time problem by replicating a model that already fits and splitting the dataset. Model parallelism tackles the memory problem by splitting a model that doesn't fit onto multiple GPUs in the first place.
